facts.statement: Remains were first mentioned in 1976, but the species was not named until 1999 when more complete fossils were found.
facts.quote: Fossils of this dinosaur were first described in 1976, but it was only named Nigersaurus taqueti in 1999 after further and more complete remains were found and described.

facts.statement: The specific name 'taqueti' honors Philippe Taquet, who discovered the initial remains.
facts.quote: the specific name honours the palaeontologist Philippe Taquet, who discovered the first remains.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus was a small sauropod, measuring between 9 and 14.1 meters in length with a short neck.
facts.quote: Small for a sauropod, Nigersaurus was about 9 - 14.1 m long, and had a short neck.

facts.statement: The animal weighed approximately 1.9 to 4 metric tons, similar to the weight of a modern elephant.
facts.quote: It weighed around 1.9 - 4 MT, comparable to a modern elephant.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus possessed a wide muzzle containing over 500 teeth that were replaced every 14 days.
facts.quote: It had a wide muzzle filled with more than 500 teeth, which were replaced at a rapid rate: around every 14 days.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus belongs to the subfamily Rebbachisaurinae of the family Rebbachisauridae within the sauropod superfamily Diplodocoidea.
facts.quote: Nigersaurus and its closest relatives are grouped within the subfamily Rebbachisaurinae (formerly thought to be grouped in the eponymous Nigersaurinae) of the family Rebbachisauridae, which is part of the sauropod superfamily Diplodocoidea.

facts.statement: Researchers believe Nigersaurus was a browser that fed on vegetation close to the ground.
facts.quote: Nigersaurus was probably a browser, and fed with its head close to the ground.

facts.statement: It inhabited a riparian environment and likely ate soft plants including ferns, horsetails, and angiosperms.
facts.quote: It lived in a riparian habitat, and its diet probably consisted of soft plants, such as ferns, horsetails, and angiosperms.

facts.statement: There is an ongoing debate regarding whether Nigersaurus held its head habitually downwards or horizontally.
facts.quote: There has been debate on whether its head was habitually held downwards, or horizontally like other sauropods.

facts.statement: Initial remains were discovered during a 1965–1972 expedition led by Philippe Taquet and first published in 1976.
facts.quote: Remains thought to belong to Nigersaurus were first discovered during a 1965–1972 expedition to the Republic of Niger led by French paleontologist Philippe Taquet, and first mentioned in a paper published in 1976.

facts.statement: The genus remained poorly known until Paul Sereno led expeditions in 1997 and 2000 that found more individuals.
facts.quote: Although a common genus, the dinosaur had been poorly known until more material of other individuals was discovered during expeditions led by American palaeontologist Paul Sereno in 1997 and 2000.

facts.statement: Fossils and a reconstructed skeleton were presented at the National Geographic Society in Washington.
facts.quote: The fossils, along with a reconstructed skeleton mount and a plastic model of the head and neck, were subsequently presented at the National Geographic Society in Washington.

facts.statement: Some skull fossils were so thin that light beams could pass through them.
facts.quote: Some of the skull fossils were so thin that a strong light beam was visible through them.

facts.statement: The press dubbed Nigersaurus a "Mesozoic cow," and Sereno considered it the most unusual dinosaur he had seen.
facts.quote: Nigersaurus was dubbed a "Mesozoic cow" in the press, and Sereno stressed that it was the most unusual dinosaur he had ever seen.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus had a body length of 9 to 14.1 meters and a femur of only 1 meter, weighing 1.9 to 4 metric tons.
facts.quote: Among that clade, Nigersaurus was fairly small, with a body length of only 9 - 14.1 m and a femur reaching only 1 m; it may have weighed around 1.9 - 4 MT, comparable to a modern elephant.

facts.statement: It possessed a short sauropod neck consisting of thirteen cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: It had a short neck for a sauropod, with thirteen cervical vertebrae.

facts.statement: The connecting bone struts in the skull were usually less than 2 millimeters thick.
facts.quote: These connecting struts of bones were usually less than 2 mm thick.

facts.statement: The maxillary tooth row was completely transversely rotated, with the rear 90 degrees everted toward the front.
facts.quote: The maxillary tooth row was in its entirety transversely rotated, its normal rear 90° everted towards the front.

facts.statement: No other tetrapod has all its teeth located as far forward as Nigersaurus due to this unique configuration.
facts.quote: Due to this configuration, no other tetrapod had all of its teeth located as far to the front as Nigersaurus.

facts.statement: Its dental batteries consisted of 68 columns in the upper jaw and 60 in the lower, totaling over 500 active and replacement teeth.
facts.quote: With 68 columns in the upper jaws and 60 columns in the lower jaws, these so-called dental batteries (also present in hadrosaurs and ceratopsians) comprised a total of more than 500 active and replacement teeth.

facts.statement: The tooth enamel was highly asymmetrical, being ten times thicker on the outer side than the inner side.
facts.quote: The enamel on the teeth of Nigersaurus was highly asymmetrical, ten times thicker on the outwards facing side than on the inner side.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus is the only known tetrapod with jaws wider than the skull and teeth extending laterally across the front.
facts.quote: Nigersaurus is the only known tetrapod animal to have had jaws wider than the skull and teeth that extended laterally across the front.

facts.statement: Grooves at the front of the jaws indicate the presence of a keratinous sheath.
facts.quote: The front ends of the jaws had grooves that indicate the presence of a keratinous (horny) sheath.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus had presacral vertebrae that were so hollow they formed a column of thin shells separated by septa.
facts.quote: The presacral vertebrae (vertebrae in front of the sacrum) were heavily pneumatised to the point where the column consisted of a series of hollow "shells", each divided by a thin septum in the middle.

facts.statement: The side walls of Nigersaurus vertebral arches were reduced to 2 mm thick ridges due to extensive air sac extensions.
facts.quote: The vertebral arches were so heavily pierced by extensions of the external air sacs that of their side walls little remained but 2 mm thick intersecting laminae, the ridges between the pneumatic openings.

facts.statement: The pelvic and pectoral girdle bones of Nigersaurus were very thin, often only a few millimeters thick.
facts.quote: The pelvic and pectoral girdle bones were very thin also, often only several millimetres thick.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus had a distinctive wrinkled area on the base of its shoulder blade.
facts.quote: It had a prominent rugosity (a roughly wrinkled area) on the midline aspect of the scapular blade's base, a distinguishing feature.

facts.statement: The front legs of Nigersaurus were approximately two-thirds the length of its hind legs.
facts.quote: The front legs of Nigersaurus were about two-thirds the length of the back legs, as in most diplodocoids.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus was originally classified as a dicraeosaurid in 1976 but was reclassified as a rebbachisaurid diplodocoid in 1999.
facts.quote: The remains of Nigersaurus were initially described by Taquet in 1976 as belonging to a dicraeosaurid, but in 1999 Sereno and colleagues reclassified it as a rebbachisaurid diplodocoid.

facts.statement: The subfamily Nigersaurinae, containing Nigersaurus, was named by John A. Whitlock in 2011.
facts.quote: The eponymous subfamily Nigersaurinae, which includes Nigersaurus and closely related genera, was named by the American palaeontologist John A. Whitlock in 2011.

facts.statement: A 2015 study suggested that Nigersaurinae might be a junior synonym of Rebbachisaurinae.
facts.quote: A 2015 cladistic study by Wilsona and the French palaeontologist Ronan Allain found Rebbachisaurus itself to group with the nigersaurines, and the authors suggested that Nigersaurinae was therefore a junior synonym of Rebbachisaurinae (since that name would have priority).

facts.statement: Despite having large nostrils, Nigersaurus had an underdeveloped olfactory brain region and likely lacked an advanced sense of smell.
facts.quote: Though it had large nostrils and a fleshy snout, Sereno and colleagues found that Nigersaurus had an underdeveloped olfactory region of its brain and thus did not have an advanced sense of smell.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus had eyes positioned high on its skull above the muzzle, providing overlapping fields of view.
facts.quote: The eyes of Nigersaurus were placed further towards the top of the skull than in most other sauropods, above the muzzle, which would give it overlapping fields of view.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus likely had a visual field close to 360 degrees, making it sensitive to movement as a vulnerable prey animal.
facts.quote: Its visual field would have been at or close to 360 degrees, and hypersensitivity of movement would have been important to a vulnerable prey-animal.

facts.statement: In 2017, researchers suggested that skeletal pneumaticity in Nigersaurus helped lower body density, reduce muscle energy needs, and dissipate heat.
facts.quote: In 2017, the Argentinian palaeontologist Lucio M. Ibiricu and colleagues examined the postcranial skeletal pneumaticity in the skeletons of rebbachisaurids, and suggested that it was an adaptation for lowering the density of the skeleton, and that this could have decreased the muscle energy needed to move the body, as well as the heat generated in the process.

facts.statement: A 2023 study conducted the first CT-scan analysis of the microanatomical structure of Nigersaurus limb bones.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that features like pneumaticity and fleshy foot pads helped reduce pressure on Nigersaurus bones, implying sauropods were lighter than expected.
facts.quote: These researchers suggested that the microanatomy of sauropods was not affected by drastic selective pressure caused by bearing weight, but that features such as the columnar limbs (as seen in elephants), pneumaticity, and fleshy foot pads and cartilage relaxed pressure on the bones.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Nigersaurus was a ground-level, non-selective browser.
facts.quote: Nigersaurus was suggested by Sereno and colleagues to be a ground-level, non-selective browser.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus could gather and crop food within 1 meter of the ground surface.
facts.quote: The width of the muzzle and lateral orientation of the tooth row show that the sauropod could gather much food and crop it close to the ground, within 1 m of the surface.

facts.statement: Nigersaurus replaced each tooth every 14 days, a rate higher than previous estimates.

facts.statement: A 2009 study contested whether the downturned head posture was the habitual one for Nigersaurus.

facts.statement: A 2020 study cautioned against using semicircular canals to infer precise skull orientation, noting the plane was not horizontal in resting poses.
